note.question: How should a retailer jointly set product price and search difficulty when the shopping process itself creates value, and when should the store intentionally make desirable items harder to find?
note.overview: A seller moves first by choosing the treasure price and discovery rate, consumers observe those choices and strategically decide whether to visit, and visitors solve a continuous-time optimal-stopping problem. The paper solves the sequential interaction by backward induction and derives the seller's profit-maximizing store design.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Stage 1: the seller chooses and publicly reveals product price p and treasure-discovery rate mu. Stage 2: consumers compare expected treasure-hunt utility U with their privately known travel cost and decide whether to visit. Stage 3: after travel cost is sunk, each visitor searches in continuous time and at every instant chooses whether to continue; a Poisson discovery ends search with purchase, otherwise the consumer stops at the optimal cutoff t*. The seller anticipates participation, stopping, and purchase probability when choosing p and mu.

models.name: Model Extensions
models.relation: This extension builds on The Joy of Shopping model.
models.summary: We now extend our model to allow for different timing of when customers learn prices, for a segment of customers who do not enjoy search, and for designing treasure hunts to cross-sell other products. In fact, for low values of the treasure, the firm sets p < 0, which implies the treasure acts as a loss leader that generates negative profit margins for the firm.9 Furthermore, the firm sets a lower treasure discovery rate than in the main model in order to provide customers with additional search utility from hunting for a treasure with higher net value.
